items.title: Northern Taurids Peak Tonight: A Natural Fireball Reference
items.body: The Northern Taurids peak November 11–12 under very favorable moonlight conditions. The shower has modest meteor rates but can produce bright fireballs. Record exact location, time, viewing direction and imagery before labeling a moving light anomalous. This is a normal astronomical event, not evidence of UAP.

items.title: NASA's November Skywatching Guide Adds a Useful Baseline
items.body: NASA projects the Northern Taurids around November 12, a Mars–Jupiter pairing on November 15–16, and Leonid activity November 17–18. These predictable events belong beside extraordinary sky reports so that a bright point, fireball or close planetary pairing is not mistaken for unexplained technology.

items.title: UAP Disclosure Advocates Keep Their Seats
items.body: Cybernews reports that Anna Paulina Luna, Tim Burchett, Eric Burlison, and Jared Moskowitz won reelection, preserving several visible bipartisan advocates for UAP disclosure in Congress. The election keeps those lawmakers in place; it does not verify UAP claims or guarantee new hearings or document releases.

items.title: Evidence Check: The “Cold Orbs” Clips Are Screen Recordings
items.body: In its August 7 release, AARO says the referenced clips were recorded from a phone filming an infrared sensor display, rather than supplied as native sensor data. It warns that this limits image fidelity and says its descriptions should not be read as an analytical conclusion about what the objects were. Preserve the case as unresolved; record the sensor chain and limits.

items.title: $100,000 Award Funds a Consciousness–UAP Research Proposal
items.body: The Institute of Noetic Sciences announced its 2026 research-prize winner on November 5: a multidisciplinary team proposing research on consciousness-associated UAP experiences. The award funds investigation; it does not establish extraterrestrial origins, paranormal mechanisms, or a validated connection.

items.title: Northern Taurids: Keep Natural Fireballs in the Reference Set
items.body: NASA's November skywatching guidance places the Northern Taurid peak around November 12. Occasional bright fireballs are expected within a generally low-rate meteor shower. Record time, location and trajectory when evaluating unusual lights; do not label an unidentified sighting exotic by default.

items.title: NASA Revisits a Major Taurid Fireball
items.body: NASA's November 8 Astronomy Picture of the Day features a 2017 fireball over the Dolomites, with reported observations consistent with the Northern Taurid meteor stream. The image is new to today's feature; the meteor itself is historical, not a fresh 2026 event.
items.source: NASA Astronomy Picture of the Day · Nov 8, 2026

items.title: Northern Taurids Near Their November Peak
items.body: NASA expects the Northern Taurids to peak around November 12. Rates are generally low—around five meteors per hour under ideal conditions—but occasional fireballs can be spectacular. A bright meteor is not, by itself, evidence of unusual technology.

items.title: A Gamma-Ray Burst Gets a Fresh Alert
items.body: The SVOM mission team reported triggering on gamma-ray burst GRB 261108A at 01:13:20 UTC on November 8, with a low-latency location estimate. This is an instrument alert from a scientific team, not a claim about danger to Earth or exotic visitors.

items.title: Black Triangle File: Observation Is Not Identification
items.body: An independent UAP weekly digest discusses disagreement over a reported black-triangle account in newly released files. Witness testimony merits preservation, but without complete sensor data and chain of evidence the object's identity remains unresolved. We should track the original record and skeptical evaluations together.
